Rokid AR Guide.

An exhibition guide that helps visitors recognize an exhibit, hear a reviewed introduction, and continue exploring through questions on smart glasses.

The case / 01

Visitors should be able to look at an exhibit and get an explanation that stays with the object they are viewing. The engineering challenge was to connect camera capture, recognition, exhibit-specific knowledge, and a readable on-glasses response into one dependable flow.

Visitor journey / illustrated

Look at an exhibit → hear its reviewed introduction → ask a follow-up question while the answer stays tied to that exhibit.

My contribution

I led the project team and integrated the Android camera pipeline with a Python service. We prioritized fresh frames so recognition would respond to what the visitor was currently seeing. I also worked on how reviewed introductions and AI-generated follow-up answers were separated, and refined the text and speech experience on the glasses.

The project combined device input, server responses, and a visitor interface. My role was to keep those parts moving together while making the interaction dependable enough for a real exhibition setting.

How the flow fits together

  • Capture: The Android camera pipeline supplies frames to the Python service, with fresher frames prioritized for recognition.
  • Context: The recognized exhibit determines which reviewed material should ground the introduction and later questions.
  • Delivery: Text and speech bring the explanation back to the visitor on the glasses.

Decisions that mattered

  • Keep the current exhibit in context. Answers need to stay tied to the recognized object, especially when a visitor moves to another exhibit.
  • Make introduction content dependable. Reviewed exhibit material and generated follow-up responses serve different purposes and were handled separately.
  • Design for the device. Short on-glasses text and speech delivery matter as much as the service response.

What was verified

Recognition, exhibit switching, and introduction playback passed user acceptance and regression checks in the internship project. The practical result was an exhibit flow that could be exercised and checked, including the handoff when a visitor moved to another exhibit.

The diagram above describes the system at a high level. It does not claim a specific recognition model, measured latency, or support for every Rokid device.
